steps.prompt: You pull socks from a dark drawer with black and white socks. How many do you need to be sure of a pair? Why is the answer not "two"?

cards.title: The worst case and the pigeonhole principle
cards.body: To be SURE of something, plan for the worst luck. The pigeonhole principle: if more than $n$ things go into $n$ boxes, some box gets two. More generally, $n(k - 1) + 1$ things in $n$ boxes force $k$ in one box.

cards.title: Worked example: socks
cards.problem: A drawer has socks in $5$ colours. How many must you take to be sure of $3$ of one colour?

steps.text: The worst case is $2$ of each colour: $10$ socks.

try.prompt: How many socks can you take with no $3$ the same?
How many socks make it certain?

cards.title: Truth-tellers, liars and orderings
cards.body: Try each case: suppose one statement is true and follow what it forces, until you reach a contradiction or a consistent story. For orderings, draw a line and place the people one clue at a time.

cards.title: Worked example: two speakers
cards.problem: Each of Ana and Bo always tells the truth or always lies. Ana says "We are both liars." Number Ana $1$ and Bo $2$: what is the sum of the numbers of the truth-tellers?

steps.text: If Ana told the truth she'd be a liar: impossible. So Ana lies.

try.prompt: Is Ana's number counted (type 1 for yes, 0 for no)?

steps.text: Since Ana lies, "we are both liars" is false, so Bo tells the truth. The sum is $2$.

cards.title: The common trap: being lucky
cards.body: "Sure" means in every case, not in a typical case. Don't count the lucky draws: count the longest run of bad luck, then add one.

prompts: How do you find the worst case in a pigeonhole problem?
